analysis.one_liner: Requires data brokers to let people see, correct, and opt out of the sale of their personal information.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that buy, assemble, and sell personal information about people who are not their customers — data brokers — would have to make sure their files are accurate, let each person review their file once a year for free and dispute errors, honor a preference not to have their information used for marketing, keep audit trails showing who accessed the data, and stop obtaining information through false pretenses. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules and maintain a public list of data brokers, and state attorneys general could sue violators for up to $16,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday people whose names, addresses, Social Security numbers, and financial details are compiled and sold by data brokers, often without their knowledge. The bill would give them a right to see what is on file, correct mistakes that can affect their ability to get a job, benefits, or services, and stop their data being used to target them. It would also protect them from brokers obtaining data by fraud.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose personal data is sold by brokers

how_it_helps.text: Requires data brokers to establish procedures to ensure the accuracy of the personal information they collect, assemble, or maintain [S2].
Gives each individual the right to review their file at least once a year at no cost and to dispute and correct inaccurate information [S2].
Prohibits data brokers from obtaining personal information by false pretenses, a common tactic in which brokers pose as customers to harvest data [S2].
Requires brokers to honor an individual's expressed preference not to have their information used, shared, or sold for marketing purposes [S2].
Requires brokers to maintain audit measures to trace internal and external access to personal data and implement a consumer privacy and data security program [S2].
Authorizes state attorneys general to sue violators on behalf of residents for civil penalties up to $16,000 per violation, adjusted for inflation [S3].
Directs the FTC to create a centralized public website listing covered data brokers and explaining consumer rights [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data broker companies, which would bear the cost of accuracy procedures, annual free file access, dispute resolution, audit systems, and potential penalties of up to $16,000 per violation. Companies that buy broker data for marketing could face smaller, costlier data pools.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data broker companies and their clients

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall most heavily on smaller data brokers, which would need new accuracy, access, dispute, and auditing systems; larger firms are better positioned to absorb them [S3].

The bill covers only a narrow set of 'personal information' — name or address combined with identifiers like a Social Security number, government ID number, or financial account number — leaving most behavioral and browsing data that brokers sell outside its scope [S3].
Individuals get no right to sue on their own; enforcement is left to the FTC and state attorneys general [S3].
Information already regulated by the Fair Credit Reporting Act is treated as compliant if the broker meets FCRA requirements, and the FTC can exempt categories of brokers by rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but modest in scope: the right to see and correct a file, opt out of marketing use, and audit access addresses harms that today have no remedy, since brokers operate with no obligation to let people see or fix their files. The narrow definition of covered information and the absence of a private right to sue mean much broker activity would continue unregulated. The main cost falls on the industry itself, which is the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 1, 2020, by Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson Jr. of Georgia, with Reps. Cohen and Cicilline, and was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1].
Those were the only cosponsors — 2 of 231 House Democrats — and no further action was ever taken on the bill [S4].
The full action history shows only introduction and committee referral; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers came out ahead: with the bill dead, they continued to compile and sell people's personal information with no obligation to ensure accuracy, provide access, honor opt-outs, or trace who accessed the data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, who faced no new obligations

for.name: Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over consumer protection legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: These companies compile and sell personal information about people who are not their customers. The bill would force accuracy procedures, annual free file access, dispute resolution, marketing opt-outs, audit trails, and exposure to $16,000-per-violation penalties — a direct hit to a business model built on selling data people never agreed to share.

Firms that buy broker data for marketing would face smaller, costlier data pools because individuals could opt out of marketing use, but the opt-out is voluntary on the consumer's part and the covered data is narrow.

Brokers handling information already covered by the Fair Credit Reporting Act are treated as compliant if they meet FCRA requirements, sparing them duplicative new obligations while leaving their existing regime in place.
